newsitem.title: UK: Hague beats Clarke to lead British Conservatives.
newsitem.headline: Hague beats Clarke to lead British Conservatives.

text.p: William Hague on Thursday became the youngest leader of Britain's Conservative party in nearly 200 years when he defeated ex-finance minister Kenneth Clarke by a surprisingly wide margin.
In a ballot of the Conservatives' 164 surviving members of parliament, Hague, won 92 votes against 70 for Clarke. Two MPs abstained or spoiled their ballot papers.

Hague, 36, succeeds former prime minister John Major, who announced his decision to step down as leader within hours of the Conservatives' crushing defeat in the May 1 election at the hands of Tony Blair's Labour party.

A beaming Hague, Welsh Secretary for two years before the election, emerged from the House of Commons to proclaim that his first task was to unite a party whose deep divisions over Europe were magnified by the leadership campaign.

"I see it as my job not only to lead the party but to heal its divisions. I owe it to every member of the party to make sure that I extend the hand of friendship and cooperation to all members of the party.

"I'm going to bring the party together. I'm going to take it back on the road to unity, to confidence and back to power -- and the whole Conservative party is now going to work together to achieve that objective," Hague said.
To underscore the point, Hague said he would offer a senior post in his "shadow" cabinet -- which will monitor the work of Blair's real cabinet -- to his defeated rival.

But Hague said Clarke, who has staked his political career on keeping open the option of joining Europe's single currency, would be expected to swallow his pride and accept Hague's line that Britain will not scrap the pound.

Conservative MPs said it appeared that Hague won comfortably because a bold bid by Clarke, the leader of the party's pro-European left wing, to forge an alliance with his ideological foe, Euro-sceptic John Redwood, had backfired.

Redwood's move was denounced by Conservative right-wingers afraid it would scupper Hague's chances and open the door to Clarke, whom they blame for the May 1 election defeat because he refused to rule out joining the single currency.
Former prime minister Margaret Thatcher spoke for many Conservatives -- and for most of Britain's newspapers -- when she dismissed it as an alliance of incredible opposites.
Although the margin of Hague's victory appeared to bode well for his intentions of uniting the party, Labour was jubilant.
It had most feared a victory by Clarke, a formidable parliamentarian with a proven track record and common touch.
"The Tory party has shown that it is more split today than ever before. They are clearly incapable of offering leadership and incapable of uniting," Trade Secretary Margaret Beckett said.

"The divisions now run so deep that these people literally hate each other. Given the loathing in the party, the idea that William Hague can put together an effective team defies credibility. After this result it is clear that William Hague will forever be the prisoner of the right," she added.
Bookmakers William Hill reacted to Hague's victory by lengthening the odds on the Conservatives winning the next election from 5/4 to 6/4. The odds on Labour shortened from 4/7 to 1/2.
